name: Nordström's Scalar Theory of Gravity
description: Gravity as one scalar field on flat spacetime, which Einstein and Fokker rewrote as a conformally flat spacetime whose curvature scalar is fixed by the trace of the stress-energy tensor of matter. Light keeps the cones of Minkowski space while clocks and rods change from place to place.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. The conformal factor $\Phi$ is a pure number, Nordström's potential divided by its value far from every mass.
history: How little can you change Newton's gravity and still square it with special relativity? Keep the potential, one number at each point of flat spacetime, and trade Poisson's equation for the wave equation, so that gravity travels at the speed of light [norton1992, norton2007]. The Finnish physicist Gunnar Nordström sent off such a theory in October 1912, promising, in John Norton's translation, to "leave $c$ constant and still adapt the theory of gravitation to the relativity principle in such a way that gravitational and inertial masses are equal" [norton2007]. Einstein had given up on a theory of that kind in 1907, and his own theory of 1912 let the speed of light vary from place to place and serve as the gravitational potential [norton2007, einstein1912].¶Einstein answered by letter before the paper was out of proof [norton2007]. Nordström reported the objection in an addendum, that "a rotating system in a gravitational field will acquire a smaller acceleration than a non-rotating system", and shrugged: "I do not find this result dubious in itself, for the difference is too small to yield a contradiction with experience" [norton2007]. Einstein's second objection was a perpetual motion machine, set out in his paper of 1913 with Marcel Grossmann under the heading "Can the gravitational field be reduced to a scalar?" [einstein1913, norton2007]. Lower some radiation in a mirrored box, raise it again between two sliding mirrors in a shaft, where it weighs a third as much, and each turn of the cycle hands you energy for nothing [norton2007]. "This seems unacceptable to me", he wrote [norton2007].¶The repair was made in Zurich in the summer of 1913, with Nordström on a visit, and he sent off his second theory on 24 July [nordstrom1913, norton2007]. Its source was the trace of the stress energy tensor, which Einstein had learned of from Max von Laue and wanted to call "Laue's scalar" [norton2007]. Its rods also grew as they fell [nordstrom1913, norton2007]. Picture a rod held taut between two rails: tension adds to its weight in this theory, so a taut rod on the way down pays out more work than a slack one takes on the way back up, unless the rod lengthens as it falls and the rails must part, which uses up the surplus exactly [norton2007]. "Herr Einstein has proved", Nordström wrote, that this "must be a general property of matter" [norton2007]. Clocks went the same way, and light from the surface of the Sun came out redder by one part in two million [nordstrom1913, norton2007].¶If every rod and every clock is off by the same factor, in what sense is the flat background there? Einstein and Adriaan Fokker, who was visiting Zurich for the winter, followed that question to its end in a paper sent off on 19 February 1914 [einstein1914fokker, norton2007]. With $\Phi$ for the factor, rods and clocks measure $ds^2 = \Phi^2(-c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)$, free fall is a geodesic of that metric, and the field equation sets the curvature scalar proportional to the trace of the stress energy tensor, $R = 24\pi G\,T/c^4$ in today's letters [einstein1914fokker, deruelle2011]. Norton calls it "the first successful field equation which set an expression in the Riemann-Christoffel curvature tensor proportional to" one in the stress energy tensor of matter, and it came twenty one months before Einstein's own [norton2007, einstein1915field].¶Light is left alone, since the factor drops out of $ds^2 = 0$: the light cones are Minkowski's everywhere, and a ray passing the Sun goes straight [einstein1914fokker, deruelle2011]. Outside a body of mass $M$ the factor is $\Phi = 1 - GM/c^2r$, clocks slow to first order as they do near Schwarzschild's mass, and a planet's perihelion creeps backwards by a sixth of Einstein's advance [deruelle2011, norton2007]. Nordström's own calculation of 1914 had the Earth's ellipse turning back by $0.0065$ seconds of arc a year, and he found the laws of fall and of planetary motion "in the best agreement with experience" [nordstrom1914, norton2007]. Where $\Phi$ reaches zero, at $r = GM/c^2$, the curvature diverges, and a body dropped in a uniform field reaches the plane where $\Phi$ vanishes in a finite time by its own clock [deruellesasaki2011, giulini2008]. The theory's universe of dust swells from a bang and falls back into a crunch whatever its density [sundrum2003].¶Einstein's finished theory accounted in November 1915 for the 43 seconds of arc a century by which Mercury's perihelion outruns Newton's prediction, and Nordström's turns the perihelion the other way [einstein1915perihelion, norton2007]. The eclipse of 29 May 1919 then showed starlight bent by $1.98$ and $1.61$ seconds of arc at the Sun's limb, where a theory with Minkowski's light cones allows none [dyson1920]. Nordström had by then moved on: in 1914 he gave spacetime a fifth dimension to make gravity and electromagnetism one field, seven years before Theodor Kaluza [nordstrom1914unify, kaluza1921, ravndal2004]. Nathalie Deruelle found a star of constant density in his scalar theory weighing exactly its total energy, gravitational binding included, and calls it "the only theory of gravity with General Relativity to obey the strong equivalence principle" [deruelle2011].

related.text: Every spacetime of Nordström's theory is $\Phi^2$ times Minkowski's metric and keeps its light cones. With no matter anywhere $\Phi = 1$, and it is Minkowski space [einstein1914fokker].

Einstein's answer to the same question, the field outside a spherical mass. To first order in $GM/c^2r$ the two slow clocks alike. Schwarzschild's field bends light and advances a perihelion by six times what Nordström's takes away [deruelle2011].
The weak field of a body with a number in front of every term. Nordström's point mass sits at $\gamma = -1$ and $\beta = 1/2$ [deruelle2011].
Nordström's universe of dust is a flat Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric in conformal time, with the scale factor $1 - c^2t^2/L^2$ his field equation picks for dust [sundrum2003].
Nordström's other spacetime. By 1918 he had taken up Einstein's theory and found in it the field of a charged mass [nordstrom1918].
Minkowski's metric times a free conformal factor again. There the factor is chosen to stretch one world line without end, and here a field equation fixes it [einstein1914fokker].

coordinates.name: Einstein-Fokker

parameters.description: Conformal factor, dimensionless and positive. It obeys Einstein and Fokker's field equation $R = 24\pi G\,T/c^4$, where $T$ is the trace of the stress-energy tensor of matter, so in a vacuum it solves the wave equation $\partial_x^2\Phi + \partial_y^2\Phi + \partial_z^2\Phi - \partial_t^2\Phi = 0$

coordinates.convention: We use Einstein and Fokker's preferred coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, in which light travels at $c$ everywhere, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, where $\partial_t = c^{-1}\partial/\partial t$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Point Mass

parameters.description: Mass of the body as a length, $m = GM/c^2$, where $M$ is its gravitational mass; half the Schwarzschild radius of the same mass

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ centred on a static spherical body, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the radius of the flat background, so that $\Phi = 1 - m/r$ and the sphere at $r$ has the area $4\pi(r - m)^2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Uniform Field

parameters.description: Proper acceleration of a body at rest at the height $z = c^2/a$, where $\Phi = 1$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $z$ the height above the plane where the conformal factor $\Phi = az/c^2$ vanishes. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Dust Universe

parameters.description: Light travel distance of half the span of the universe in the inertial time, $L = c/\sqrt{2\pi G\rho_0}$, where $\rho_0$ is the density of the dust at its greatest expansion, $t = 0$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ in which the dust is at rest, with $t$ the inertial time of the flat background, carrying dimensions of time, and $r$ a comoving radius. The conformal factor $\Phi = 1 - c^2t^2/L^2$ is the scale factor. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
